claims.text: Controlled SRO introduced by dual-stage annealing will improve the combined strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance of an FCC alloy relative to its homogenized disordered state.
Equiatomic CrCoNi has an FCC structure.
CrCoNi is an example of a high-entropy alloy.
Hot rolling produces a largely homogeneous, disordered solid-solution microstructure in the target alloy.
A high-temperature homogenization treatment removes segregation from the target alloy.
A subsequent lower-temperature, medium-duration heat treatment can induce SRO in CoCrNi.
The proposed second-stage anneal can induce SRO without precipitating secondary phases.
Atom probe tomography can measure species-specific SRO and monitor changes caused by heat treatments in CoCrNi.
Preliminary atom probe tomography can determine a processing threshold that induces SRO while retaining the FCC phase.
The dual-stage treatment will produce nanoscale SRO clusters within the FCC matrix.
SRO clusters locally impede dislocation motion.
Dislocation impediment by SRO promotes work hardening and increases yield strength.
SRO-induced work hardening increases fracture resistance.
Avoiding coarse precipitation and catastrophic phase decomposition preserves high intrinsic ductility.
Avoiding coarse precipitation and catastrophic phase decomposition preserves high Young’s modulus.
The treated alloy will show increased yield strength and fracture toughness while maintaining or modestly increasing ductility and Young’s modulus.
The method is applicable only to single-phase FCC alloys with an intrinsic tendency to develop SRO during controlled thermal exposure.
Unwanted precipitation, grain coarsening, or failure to develop appreciable SRO will prevent the proposed benefit.
The optimal annealing window is uncertain and may vary with alloy composition.
